questions.stem: A university library is replacing its room-booking system. The signed requirements document describes screen mechanics in detail: a drop-down listing every bookable room, a confirmation dialogue, a printable slip. Reading it with the librarian who commissioned the work, you learn the actual problem is that the two accessible study rooms are regularly double-booked and nobody notices until a student arrives. The supplier has priced the document as written and wants to start next week. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Let the supplier build what the signed document specifies, since it was agreed and priced.
options.rationale: The error is treating a signature as proof that the right thing was written down. A document can be agreed by everyone and still describe a solution nobody needed, and the signature makes that harder to unpick later, not easier.

options.text: Restate the requirements as the needs and outcomes they exist to serve, confirm them with the same people who signed, and baseline that version before build starts.
options.rationale: Requirements stated as needs let the supplier propose a mechanism and let everyone test whether the delivered thing worked. Re-confirming with the original signatories keeps the agreement intact rather than substituting your reading for theirs.

options.text: Leave the document alone and ask the supplier to suggest better mechanisms during detailed design.
options.rationale: This hands the definition of the need to the party with the least interest in narrowing it, and it happens after the price is fixed. Design conversations cannot repair a specification that never said what problem it was solving.

options.text: Build as specified and raise a change request once users report that double bookings still occur.
options.rationale: Choosing this accepts paying twice for one outcome, and it deliberately defers a known defect in the requirements to the most expensive point at which to find it. Knowing now and acting later is a decision, not a discovery.

questions.explanation: A requirement should say what must be true for the work to be worth doing; a specification of screen mechanics says how somebody imagined achieving it. When the two are confused, the project can deliver every line of the document and still leave the original problem untouched, and nobody can prove it has failed because the document was met. Agreement on a solution is not agreement on a need, and only one of the two can be tested after delivery.
questions.mindset: Agree what must become true before agreeing what will be built.

questions.stem: A tyre-fitting chain has contracted you to replace its branch booking system. The scope statement lists the deliverables and says nothing about the four legacy branch price lists. At the first design workshop the client's operations manager refers in passing to the price lists being converted, while your delivery lead has estimated on the basis that the client loads them. Roughly three weeks of effort sits between the two readings. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Absorb the conversion as a goodwill gesture to keep the relationship warm this early in the work.
options.rationale: The error is buying goodwill with unpriced effort at the point when the pattern for the whole engagement is being set. Every later ambiguity now has a precedent pointing at you.

options.text: Tell the client the conversion is out of scope because the scope statement does not mention it.
options.rationale: Silence in a document proves nothing about what was intended, so this asserts a conclusion the evidence does not support. It also spends the relationship defending a reading rather than settling the question.

options.text: Take the ambiguity to the client now, agree which party converts the price lists, and record the answer either as a named deliverable or as a stated exclusion.
options.rationale: The gap is that nobody decided, and either decision is survivable once it is written down. Recording an exclusion is as much a scope activity as recording a deliverable, and it is the half most often skipped.

options.text: Escalate to your sponsor for a ruling on who is contractually responsible.
options.rationale: This routes a decision two people in the room can make through someone who was not there. It also produces a position rather than an agreement, and the client is still free to read the silence their own way.

questions.explanation: A scope statement is read most closely at the moments when money depends on it, and what it omits is where those readings diverge. Stating exclusions is not defensive drafting; it is the only way a reader can tell a deliberate boundary from an oversight. An ambiguity found early costs a conversation, and the same ambiguity found at acceptance costs a dispute, so the value of settling it falls sharply with time.
questions.mindset: Write down what you are not delivering, because silence is read as agreement by whoever it suits.

questions.stem: Your veterinary diagnostics laboratory has built a sample-tracking module. Your quality team tested it against the specification, found no outstanding defects and signed it off internally. At the customer walkthrough, the practice manager says the module cannot record a sample that arrives split across two containers, which happens several times a week. Your business analyst believes this was never written down. The customer expects the module to be accepted this week. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Point out that the internal quality sign-off is complete and ask the customer to accept on that basis.
options.rationale: This conflates checking a deliverable against its specification with the customer agreeing the deliverable is what they asked for. They are different questions and only the customer can answer the second one.

options.text: Log the split-container handling as a defect and put it into the next rework cycle.
options.rationale: Labelling it a defect assumes the requirement existed and was missed. If nobody ever specified it, the label quietly transfers the cost of a requirements gap onto the delivery team and hides the gap from everyone.

options.text: Take the module back to its recorded acceptance criteria, separate what fails a criterion from what no criterion covers, and re-run acceptance once each part has an agreed route.
options.rationale: The two categories have different owners, different costs and different remedies, and only the criteria can tell them apart. Sorting them before negotiating stops one conversation being settled on the terms of the other.

options.text: Ask the customer to accept the module now with the split-container issue recorded on a snag list.
options.rationale: This buys a signature by deferring the substantive question, and a snag list is a poor container for something that may be new scope. The acceptance record then shows agreement that nobody actually gave.

questions.explanation: Verification asks whether the deliverable matches what was specified; acceptance asks whether the customer agrees it is what they wanted. Passing the first is a precondition for asking the second, never a substitute for it. When acceptance surfaces something the criteria never mentioned, the useful move is to establish which side of that line it falls on, because a missed requirement and a failed one are paid for by different people and fixed by different routes.
questions.mindset: Before arguing about who pays, establish whether the thing was specified at all.

questions.stem: A county records office is having its photographic index digitised. After an emailed demonstration, an archivist replied "looks great to me", and your team recorded the indexing deliverable as accepted and moved on. Six weeks later the head of archives, who is named in the acceptance plan as the signatory, says the deliverable is unacceptable because the date-range search she specified is missing. Your team has since built two further deliverables on top of it. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Hold the customer to the archivist's email, since it was a clear written statement of satisfaction.
options.rationale: The error is treating enthusiasm from anyone in the customer organisation as an exercise of acceptance authority. Approval given by someone without standing to give it binds nobody, however warmly it was worded.

options.text: Re-run acceptance with the named signatory against the recorded criteria, and correct the acceptance route so the team knows who can accept what.
options.rationale: It puts the deliverable back in front of the only person whose agreement counts, and fixes the mechanism that allowed an informal comment to be booked as a decision. Both halves are needed or the same thing happens again.

options.text: Treat the deliverable as accepted and raise the date-range search as a change request.
options.rationale: This converts your own process failure into new scope the customer is asked to fund. If the search was in the criteria, it was never new, and calling it a change is an argument you will lose slowly and expensively.

options.text: Escalate to the sponsor and ask them to confirm the email as valid acceptance.
options.rationale: Asking a sponsor to ratify a defective acceptance spends credibility defending the weakest part of your own process, and it invites scrutiny of every other deliverable accepted the same way.

questions.explanation: Acceptance is an act performed by a named authority against recorded criteria, not a sentiment expressed by whoever saw the work first. Where the two are confused, a project accumulates deliverables it believes are closed and the customer believes are open, and the divergence surfaces at the worst possible moment. The cost of re-running one acceptance is small; the cost of discovering at handover that the acceptance record was never valid is not.
questions.mindset: Only the person named to accept can accept, and everything else is feedback.

questions.stem: You are letting the automation package for a glasshouse tomato grower's packhouse. Two shortlisted suppliers have priced the same work package, described in your work breakdown structure only as "packing line integration", and their prices differ by £40,000. Your engineering lead says both firms are competent and both day rates are similar. The evaluation panel meets in a week and wants a recommendation. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Write the dictionary entry for the disputed package, stating the deliverable, its boundaries, its acceptance criteria and what it excludes, and re-price against it.
options.rationale: The dictionary entry is the artifact that turns a package name into something two parties can price identically. Without it the tender is asking for numbers against a phrase, and any comparison between them is meaningless.

options.text: Ask each supplier what they assumed the package included, to establish whether the gap is scope or rate.
options.rationale: It tests the actual hypothesis before spending money on it. A gap made of assumptions is fixed by defining the work; a gap made of rates is a commercial conversation, and the remedies do not overlap.

options.text: Recommend the lower price and manage any missing work through the contract during delivery.
options.rationale: Choosing this treats a definition problem as a negotiating win, and it buys a dispute at the exact point where you have least leverage. The cheaper bid is often cheaper because it assumed less was included.

options.text: Take the midpoint of the two bids as the estimate for the package.
options.rationale: Averaging two answers to a question of definition produces a number that describes nobody's scope. It also disguises the disagreement as a range, so nobody investigates it.

options.text: Decompose the package into further levels of the work breakdown structure until the difference disappears.
options.rationale: More levels add detail without adding definition; the boundary and the acceptance test are what is missing, not depth. Decomposing an undefined package produces several undefined smaller ones.

questions.explanation: A work breakdown structure names the work, and the dictionary is what makes each name mean the same thing to everyone pricing, planning or accepting it. Where two competent parties price the same package very differently, the usual cause is not commercial but definitional, and the test is to establish what each assumed before treating the difference as money. Detail and definition are not the same thing, and only one of them settles an argument.
questions.mindset: When two people price the same words differently, suspect the words before you suspect the prices.

questions.stem: A prison education service's learner records replacement has been re-baselined twice, each time through the proper approval route, and the current baseline is smaller than the original by two significant modules. Your reports show every measure green against that baseline. The sponsor, who approved both changes at busy board meetings a year apart, tells a funders' panel that the project is on track to deliver everything promised in the original business case. You are asked to prepare next month's report. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Continue reporting against the current baseline, since governance requires performance to be measured against the approved plan.
options.rationale: The error is letting procedural correctness stand in for a true picture. Every number is defensible while the report as a whole tells a funder something the project manager knows to be false.

options.text: Report against the original baseline so that the shortfall against the business case is visible.
options.rationale: This discards decisions the organisation properly made and holds the team accountable for scope it was told to stop delivering. Accuracy about the commitment is not achieved by pretending the changes did not happen.

options.text: Report performance against the current baseline while showing the original commitment and the approved changes that moved it, so the gap between the two is on the page.
options.rationale: It keeps the measurement honest and the history visible in the same document, so nobody has to reconstruct the trail from memory. The sponsor is then correcting a public statement with evidence rather than being contradicted.

options.text: Ask the sponsor which of the two baselines they would prefer the report to use.
options.rationale: Offering the audience a choice of measuring stick invites them to pick the flattering one, and it makes the project manager complicit in whatever they choose. Reporting standards are not a matter of preference.

questions.explanation: A baseline is the reference for measuring performance, not the record of what was promised, and after several approved changes those two things describe different projects. A report that shows only current performance is accurate and still misleading, because the reader supplies the original commitment from memory. Carrying the trail of approved change alongside the measurement is what lets a governance body see both that the team is performing and that the deal has moved.
questions.mindset: Measure against the current baseline and show what moved it, because the reader is comparing you to the promise.

questions.stem: A botanic garden is replacing its membership system. The sponsor forwards you an email from the trustees and asks you to reply confirming that gift-aid reclaim reporting will be delivered, as the business case describes. You recall discussing gift aid during requirements workshops but cannot remember how it was settled, and the scope statement on your desk does not obviously mention it. The sponsor would like the reply sent today. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Check the scope baseline and requirements documentation, then tell the sponsor whether gift-aid reporting is in scope, excluded, or never decided.
options.rationale: The question is one of record, and the record is a short walk away. Answering with what was agreed, including the possibility that nothing was, is the only reply that stays true after it is forwarded to trustees.

options.text: Confirm it, because the business case describes it and the business case is the senior document.
options.rationale: A business case states why the investment is worth making, not what the project agreed to build. Treating it as the scope record commits the team to anything a benefits author once imagined.

options.text: Reply that it is not in scope, since it does not appear in the scope statement.
options.rationale: Answering from a quick glance risks denying a commitment that exists elsewhere in the requirements, and a written denial to trustees is expensive to withdraw.

options.text: Ask the delivery team whether they could fit gift-aid reporting in before the deadline.
options.rationale: This turns a question about what was agreed into a question about capacity, and a yes would create scope by accident without anyone approving it.

questions.explanation: Questions of the form "are we delivering X?" are answered from the scope baseline, not from memory, goodwill or the business case, and the honest answer is sometimes that the point was never settled. Saying so early converts a future dispute into a present decision. A project manager who answers such questions from recollection eventually confirms something nobody agreed, in writing, to an audience that keeps it.
questions.mindset: Answer questions about what was agreed from the record, never from memory.

questions.stem: A school meals service is refitting a central production kitchen. The control account for the refrigeration branch of the work breakdown structure is budgeted at £680,000. Its work packages are budgeted at £210,000 for cold room construction, £165,000 for chiller plant, £120,000 for controls and monitoring, and £95,000 for commissioning. Your planner says the branch is complete and ready to baseline. Work out what the numbers say before you agree.

blanks.label: Budget in the control account not accounted for by any work package, in £
blanks.rationale: The four packages total £590,000 against a control account of £680,000, leaving £90,000 attached to no package. Money in a parent that appears in no child is work nobody has been made responsible for.

blanks.label: That unaccounted budget as a percentage of the control account, to one decimal place
blanks.rationale: 90,000 ÷ 680,000 is 13.2 per cent. Expressing the gap as a share shows whether it is a rounding artefact or, as here, a material block of scope with no owner and no acceptance test.

blanks.label: The decomposition rule this branch breaks by leaving budget in the parent
blanks.rationale: Decomposition holds only if the children account for all of the parent and nothing more. A branch that leaves 13 per cent in the parent is not complete, whatever the planner's confidence about it.

questions.explanation: A work breakdown structure is a claim that the children of every node add up to that node exactly, and the claim is checkable by arithmetic before anyone argues about it. Budget stranded in a parent means either that work has been forgotten or that effort is being held back from scrutiny, and both are found the same way. Running the roll-up is a cheaper form of review than reading the structure for plausibility.
questions.mindset: Add up a breakdown before you believe it, because completeness is arithmetic rather than opinion.

questions.stem: Three disagreements have surfaced in the same fortnight on a cinema chain's projection upgrade, and all three are currently being argued from memory in meetings, with each party equally certain and none of them citing anything written down. Match each disagreement to the artifact that can actually settle it, rather than to the person arguing hardest. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: The client insists a bilingual subtitle interface was agreed at a workshop last spring; your team has no record of it and it appears in no estimate.
The screen refit lead and the network lead each believe the other's package delivers the fire alarm interlock, and neither has planned it.
A tester cannot say whether the projector's failure to handle a mid-film format switch is a defect or behaviour that was never asked for.

options.text: The requirements documentation and its sign-off history
options.rationale: A claim that something was agreed is settled by the record of what was agreed and by whom, with versions and dates. Workshop recollection a year later is evidence of intent at best, and both parties usually remember sincerely.

options.text: The work breakdown structure dictionary entries for the two packages
options.rationale: The dictionary states each package's boundary and what it excludes, which is exactly the question two owners are disagreeing about. If neither entry mentions the interlock, the gap is real and now visible.

options.text: The recorded acceptance criteria for that deliverable
options.rationale: Whether something is a defect depends on whether it was required, and the criteria are where that was written down. Without them the tester is being asked to make a scope decision from the test bench.

options.text: The change log
options.rationale: Not used. A change log shows what was altered after agreement, and none of these three is about an alteration; all three are about what was agreed in the first place. Reaching for it here answers a question nobody asked.

questions.explanation: Scope artifacts are not filing for its own sake; each answers a different question that predictably becomes a dispute. Who agreed to this, where does one package stop and the next begin, and what would count as done are three separate questions, and reaching for the wrong artifact makes an argument last longer. The value of the record shows up in the fortnight when several of these arrive at once and memory is the only alternative.
questions.mindset: Keep the record that answers the argument you can see coming.

questions.stem: An optician chain's lens-ordering replacement has reached formal acceptance of its first two deliverables, and both have run into difficulty in the same week for quite different reasons. The customer's representative is willing to talk but wants matters closed quickly. Complete each sentence with the response that fits the situation described. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: The customer's representative will not sign for a deliverable that meets every recorded criterion, because a different deliverable is four weeks late. The project manager should
A deliverable misses one recorded criterion, the customer calls the shortfall trivial and offers to sign anyway. The project manager should

options.text: record that the criteria are met, and raise the withheld signature as an issue in its own right
options.rationale: Acceptance is a judgement about one deliverable against its criteria, and letting an unrelated grievance attach to it makes every future acceptance a negotiation about everything else. The lateness is real and needs its own route.

options.text: record the shortfall and the customer's decision to accept it explicitly before taking the signature
options.rationale: A signature that quietly covers an unmet criterion leaves no trace of what was waived, and trivial in March is often material in September when a different person is reading the file.

options.text: hold the deliverable back from acceptance until every deliverable is complete
options.rationale: Not used. Batching acceptance to the end removes the benefit of accepting incrementally and replaces many small decisions with one large one, taken when there is no time to act on it.

questions.explanation: Formal acceptance works because it is narrow: this deliverable, these criteria, this authority, recorded. Both common distortions widen it — one lets an unrelated dispute hold a sound deliverable hostage, the other lets a sound signature cover an unrecorded shortfall. Keeping the acceptance record faithful to what was actually met, and dealing with everything else through its own route, is what makes the record worth having later.
questions.mindset: Keep acceptance about the deliverable in front of you, and write down anything you agreed to overlook.

questions.stem: The diagram shows the boundary of the new ticketing system for a public aquarium, with the four external systems it must exchange data with. Your scope statement names three of these interfaces as deliverables and your work breakdown structure has a package for each of those three. The system cannot go live without all four. Select the interface that the project is depending on but has not made anyone responsible for.

graphic.title: Ticketing system boundary with four external interfaces
graphic.caption: Select an interface. Use Tab or the arrow keys to move between them, then Enter or Space.

regions.label: Card acquirer — payment authorisation
regions.rationale: This interface is named in the scope statement and has its own work package with an owner and an estimate. It is a dependency, but it is a managed one, which is the difference that matters here.

regions.label: Membership database — entitlement lookup
regions.rationale: Also named and packaged. It is easy to select because entitlement logic is the most complex of the four, but complexity is not the question being asked; ownership is.

regions.label: Turnstiles — barcode validation
regions.rationale: Named in the scope statement and carried by the gate hardware package. Its supplier is contracted, so a problem here would surface as a supplier issue rather than as an unowned gap.

regions.label: Finance ledger — daily takings posting
regions.rationale: Nothing in the scope statement or the breakdown covers this interface, yet the aquarium cannot reconcile a day's takings without it. Unowned interfaces are typically the dull ones that sit between two departments rather than between two suppliers.

questions.explanation: A scope boundary is only as good as the interfaces drawn across it, and the ones that go missing are rarely the technically interesting ones. They are the interfaces to systems nobody in the room represents, which is why drawing the boundary with the operational picture in front of you catches more than reviewing the breakdown alone. An interface with no work package has no owner, no estimate and no acceptance test, whatever the architecture assumes about it.
questions.mindset: Every line crossing your boundary needs a name against it, or the system will need something nobody is building.

questions.stem: A professional body is replacing its membership renewal system. The scope statement records an assumption that the body will supply cleansed member data in an agreed format. Six weeks into build, the first extract arrives with duplicate records, missing postcodes and three different date conventions. The membership director says nobody there was ever asked to do cleansing work and there is no budget for it. Your build team is idle from Monday. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Have the team cleanse the data so the schedule holds, and mention it in the monthly report.
options.rationale: This absorbs a material piece of unbudgeted scope in order to protect a date, and reporting it afterwards is not the same as anyone deciding it. The next assumption in the document also then goes untested.

options.text: Raise it as a scope change with its cost and schedule impact, and review the remaining assumptions in the scope statement for the same weakness.
options.rationale: It puts a real decision in front of the people who can fund it, and it treats the failure as evidence about the document rather than as one bad day. Assumptions written without an owner tend to arrive in batches.

options.text: Hold the membership director to the assumption recorded in the scope statement.
options.rationale: An assumption is a statement of what the project decided to believe, not an obligation anyone accepted. Treating it as a commitment argues with a party whose agreement you never actually obtained.

options.text: Log a risk for data quality and continue building against the sample data you already hold.
options.rationale: The event has happened, so it is an issue and logging it as a risk delays the decision by a reporting cycle. Building on sample data also guarantees rework at the point of real migration.

questions.explanation: An assumption in a scope statement records something the plan depends on but nobody has confirmed, which makes it a piece of scope waiting for an owner. The useful discipline is to name who has agreed to make each assumption true and by when, because an unowned assumption is simply undiscovered work with a date attached. When one fails, it is worth reading the rest of the list, since they were usually written in the same session and the same spirit.
questions.mindset: Treat every assumption as work somebody has to do, and find out who agreed to do it.

questions.stem: A car auction house commissioned an online bidding platform. During requirements work, users spent three afternoons with a clickable prototype and enthusiastically approved it. The written requirements were produced afterwards and signed. Your team built to the document. At the first user session, bidders say the bidding increments behave differently from the prototype they agreed, and they are right; the document says something else on several points. Both records are in circulation. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Build to the signed requirements, since they are the baselined record and the prototype was only illustrative.
options.rationale: Defensible on paper and wrong about what happened: the users gave their agreement to the prototype, and the document was written after the fact. Being right about which artifact was baselined does not make the delivered behaviour acceptable.

options.text: Build to the prototype, since that is what the users actually reviewed and agreed.
options.rationale: This lets an unbaselined artifact silently become the specification. Nobody costed the prototype's behaviour, and its differences from the document have never been individually agreed by anyone accountable.

options.text: Put the two records side by side, resolve each difference explicitly with the signatories, and re-baseline one of them as the governing record.
options.rationale: The differences are decisions that were never consciously taken, and taking them one at a time is the only way to price them. Naming one governing record afterwards stops the same ambiguity regenerating.

options.text: Treat every difference between the prototype and the delivered system as a defect and schedule rework.
options.rationale: Calling it a defect assumes the prototype was the requirement, which is the very question in dispute. It also commits to rework before anyone has decided which behaviour the business actually wants.

questions.explanation: A project can end up with two records of what was agreed: the one people signed and the one they actually looked at. Prototypes earn their keep because users engage with them, and that same quality makes them a de facto specification unless the written record is reconciled against them while the memory is fresh. When two records disagree, the work is to decide each difference deliberately rather than to argue about which artifact has more authority.
questions.mindset: Whatever the customer actually looked at is what they agreed to, so make the written record match it.

questions.stem: A fire and rescue service is upgrading eleven stations under your programme. A different programme has overrun and your sponsor asks you to take twenty per cent out of your scope to release funds, naming the percentage rather than any deliverable. Two of your eleven stations are being upgraded to meet a statutory breathing-apparatus storage requirement with a fixed compliance date. The sponsor wants your proposal in a week. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Come back with named deliverables that could be removed and the specific consequence of removing each, rather than a percentage.
options.rationale: A percentage is a budget instruction; scope is made of things. Converting one into the other is the project manager's job, and it lets the sponsor choose consequences instead of choosing arithmetic.

options.text: Establish which commitments are statutory or contractual and therefore not available to be cut, before proposing anything.
options.rationale: Some scope cannot be traded whatever the funding pressure, and finding that out after the proposal is circulated wastes the week and the credibility. It also narrows the field the sponsor is choosing from to a real one.

options.text: Apply the reduction evenly across all eleven stations so that no station is singled out.
options.rationale: Even cuts feel fair and are indifferent to value, taking the same slice from the most and least useful work. They also tend to leave every station partly finished, which delivers nothing anywhere.

options.text: Move twenty per cent of the scope into a future phase that has not yet been funded.
options.rationale: Deferral without funding is a cut wearing a disguise, and it lets everyone avoid the decision while the expectation of delivery survives. The reckoning simply moves to a later, quieter meeting.

options.text: Ask each workstream lead to volunteer twenty per cent of their own scope for removal.
options.rationale: This turns a value judgement into a negotiation between people with unequal standing and incomplete pictures, and the scope that survives is the scope with the best-defended owner.

questions.explanation: A funding instruction expressed as a percentage is not yet a scope decision, and translating it into named deliverables with named consequences is what allows the decision to be taken by someone with authority over the consequences. The translation also surfaces the parts of scope that are not discretionary at all. Uniform reductions and unfunded deferrals are both ways of appearing to answer while leaving the real choice untaken.
questions.mindset: Turn a percentage into a list of things and their consequences before anyone agrees to it.

questions.stem: At a portfolio forum you see the scope of another project in your further education college's programme. Its second deliverable is a student identity card interface that is also in your scope statement, described differently but plainly the same integration. Both projects have baselined scope and both have the work starting next term. The other project manager has not noticed. Neither sponsor is in the room. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Carry on, since your project is further advanced and will reach the interface first.
options.rationale: This settles a portfolio question by whoever moves fastest, and it spends college money building one thing twice while both baselines still say it is owed.

options.text: Remove the interface from your scope so that the duplication is resolved without argument.
options.rationale: Unilateral removal leaves a hole if the other project later descopes or slips, and the college has no record of who now owes the interface. Quiet withdrawal is not a decision anyone can rely on.

options.text: Raise the overlap at portfolio level with both scope statements, so that one project is named as owner and the other's baseline is formally changed.
options.rationale: The overlap exists between two approved baselines, so only the level that approved them can resolve it and record which one moved. That record is what protects both projects at acceptance.

options.text: Agree informally with the other project manager which of you will build it.
options.rationale: A handshake between two managers leaves two baselines saying something neither intends to do, and it survives only as long as both of them stay in post.

questions.explanation: Two projects in one portfolio can each hold a correct, approved scope and still overlap, because scope is agreed vertically with a sponsor and duplication is only visible horizontally. When it appears, the resolution has to happen where both baselines can be changed, and it has to end in a record; an informal division of labour leaves documents that contradict the intention of the people relying on them.
questions.mindset: Overlaps between baselines get resolved where the baselines were approved, not between the two managers.

questions.stem: A canal trust has given you the breakdown for a lock refurbishment. Most of its lowest level reads as deliverables: gate assemblies, masonry repairs, hydraulic installation, towpath reinstatement. One package reads "monitor contractor performance" and carries eleven months of effort. Your planner argues the work is real, someone has to do it, and it therefore belongs in the structure. The estimate is being reviewed on Thursday. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Leave the package as it is, because the effort is genuine and removing it would understate the cost.
options.rationale: The effort being genuine is not the test. A package with no deliverable can never be finished, measured or accepted, so it will report as in progress for eleven months and tell nobody anything.

options.text: Delete the package, since monitoring is management activity rather than project scope.
options.rationale: Deleting it removes real effort from the estimate and the schedule. The rule that children must account for the whole parent works in both directions, and understating is as damaging as overstating.

options.text: Recast the effort so it produces something completable, such as the monthly performance reports, or carry it where management effort is properly held.
options.rationale: It keeps the cost in the estimate while giving the work a completion test, which is what makes progress against it meaningful. Either home is defensible; leaving an unfinishable package in the structure is not.

options.text: Move the item to the risk register, since contractor performance is a risk to the project.
options.rationale: A category error: the risk is that the contractor performs badly, while the item is the effort of watching. Moving work to a risk register makes it disappear from the estimate without reducing it.

questions.explanation: Every element at the bottom of a breakdown should be something that can be finished, handed over and judged complete, because that is what turns the structure into a way of measuring progress rather than a list of activities. Ongoing effort is real and belongs in the cost, but it needs either an output that completes or a home outside the deliverable structure. The question to ask of any package is what would exist when it is done.
questions.mindset: If a package can never be finished, it cannot tell you anything about progress.

questions.stem: A climbing gym's membership app is built by a team that moves cards to a Done column when the developer and reviewer are satisfied. The product owner sees the work for the first time at the review each fortnight, and in the last two reviews she has rejected three items for missing behaviour that the acceptance criteria describe. The team is frustrated at rework landing so late; the product owner is frustrated at seeing surprises. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Add a product owner approval column to the board before Done, so nothing moves without her.
options.rationale: This makes the product owner a queue and moves the delay rather than removing it. It also treats the problem as a missing gate when the criteria were already written and simply were not checked.

options.text: Agree that an item is not done until its acceptance criteria have been confirmed with the product owner, and have that confirmation happen as each item finishes rather than at the review.
options.rationale: It moves the conversation to the point where the work is fresh and the cost of change is lowest, and it makes Done mean agreed rather than submitted. The review then shows working software instead of settling disputes.

options.text: Treat the review as the acceptance point and plan capacity for the rework it generates.
options.rationale: Budgeting for predictable rework normalises a two-week feedback delay. It also turns the review into a negotiation, which is the one thing that reliably stops other stakeholders attending it.

options.text: Ask the product owner to write more detailed acceptance criteria for future items.
options.rationale: The criteria here were adequate; nobody read them before calling the work finished. Responding to a confirmation failure with more documentation adds effort without touching the cause.

questions.explanation: Done is a claim that work is finished, and the claim is only useful if the person who can confirm it has done so. Where confirmation is batched to a single event, feedback arrives at the maximum distance from the work and the event stops being a demonstration and becomes an inspection. The fix is nearly always to move confirmation closer to completion rather than to add a stage that formalises the gap.
questions.mindset: Confirm work is finished with the person who decides, at the moment it is finished.

questions.stem: A city bike-hire scheme's app team picks up a story about warning riders when a docking station is full. Its acceptance criteria specify a red banner at the top of the screen carrying a particular sentence. A developer points out that riders are usually looking at the map, and proposes marking full stations on the map itself. The product owner replies that the criteria are the criteria and were agreed with the operations team. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Have the team build the banner exactly as the criteria describe, since the criteria were agreed.
options.rationale: It implements a design decision the criteria author probably did not know they were making, and it spends the team's knowledge of the product on nothing. Agreement on wording is not agreement that the wording is right.

options.text: Work with the product owner to restate the criteria as the rider behaviour to be achieved and how it will be observed, leaving the mechanism to the team.
options.rationale: Criteria that describe an outcome can be tested and can accommodate a better mechanism, and reworking them with the product owner keeps the operations team's intent intact rather than overriding it.

options.text: Build the banner now and raise the map idea as a separate backlog item for later.
options.rationale: This pays twice for one behaviour and ships something the team already believes will not work. The second item will also compete against new features and probably lose.

options.text: Let the team build the map marking, since they understand the product better than the criteria author.
options.rationale: Being right about the mechanism does not confer authority to change what was agreed. Unilateral substitution teaches the operations team that written criteria do not survive contact with the team.

questions.explanation: Acceptance criteria that specify a mechanism quietly transfer design authority to whoever wrote them, usually without their realising it, and they cannot be met a better way. Criteria that state the outcome and how it would be observed keep the decision where the knowledge is while remaining testable. The repair is a conversation with the person who owns the intent, not a decision taken around them.
questions.mindset: Write criteria that say what must be true, not how someone imagined achieving it.

questions.stem: An ambulance service's shift-swap tool is being built by your team. Four days into a two-week iteration, the pair working on the swap-approval story find that two supervisors can approve the same swap at once, leaving a rota short. Handling that was never discussed and is not in the criteria, but without it the feature cannot safely be used. The work looks like three or four days. The iteration ends on Friday week. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Have the team absorb the extra work quietly so the iteration commitment is still met.
options.rationale: Hiding the work protects a number at the cost of the record, so future forecasts are built on iterations that contained more than they appeared to. It also removes the product owner's chance to decide.

options.text: Bring the discovery to the product owner now and separate what the agreed criteria require from what would be genuinely new behaviour, then decide together what stays in the iteration.
options.rationale: It is a scope question with a real cost, and the person who orders the backlog should take it while there is still iteration left to act on. Splitting understood-better from asked-for-more is what makes the decision possible.

options.text: Raise a change request so the additional work is formally assessed and approved.
options.rationale: It imports a baseline mechanism into a setting that already has a faster one. The backlog and its owner exist precisely so that this decision does not need a committee.

options.text: Drop the story from the iteration and re-plan the remaining days around other items.
options.rationale: Over-correction: discovery inside a story is ordinary, and abandoning the story wastes four days of work and delays a feature the service needs. The story may still be finishable once the scope question is settled.

questions.explanation: Work that emerges mid-iteration is either the agreed scope understood more accurately or an addition to it, and the two are handled differently even though they feel identical to the team doing them. Making the distinction out loud with the person who owns the ordering keeps estimates honest and keeps the decision with whoever bears the consequence. The failure mode is silence, because a team that absorbs emergent work teaches everyone that its numbers mean less than they seem to.
questions.mindset: Say out loud whether new work is the same scope understood better or more scope, and let the owner decide.

questions.stem: A theatre's box-office product team is halfway through a review when the chief executive, attending for the first time, says a donor-recognition feature must be in this iteration because a fundraising gala falls in three weeks. The product owner is in the room and has not spoken. The team has six days of the iteration left and a full commitment. Everyone is waiting for someone to answer. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Have the request captured as a backlog item and ask the product owner to order it against the current work, in the room.
options.rationale: It treats a senior request the same way as any other while making the ordering visible to the person making it. Doing it in the room means the chief executive sees the trade rather than hearing about it later.

options.text: If it genuinely cannot wait, ask the product owner which committed item it would replace.
options.rationale: Urgency is a real input and the honest response is a swap rather than an addition. Naming what leaves makes the cost of the gala deadline explicit to the person who set it.

options.text: Accept the request into the iteration, since the chief executive outranks everyone present.
options.rationale: Authority over the organisation is not authority over the ordering of the backlog, and one override in public tells every stakeholder that seniority is the fastest route into an iteration.

options.text: Explain that iteration scope is fixed once committed and the request must wait for the next planning session.
options.rationale: Quoting a rule at a legitimate business deadline mistakes a working agreement for a constraint of nature. Iteration scope can change; the point is that it changes through the product owner and with something given up.

options.text: Add the feature and extend the iteration by a week so the gala date is met.
options.rationale: Stretching the cadence to fit unplanned work hides the scope decision inside a timing change and destroys the comparability of every forecast built on iteration length.

questions.explanation: Requests from senior people are not a different category of request; what changes is the pressure to skip the ordering step. The response that survives repetition is to make the request visible, make the trade-off visible and leave the decision with the person accountable for value. Where genuine urgency exists, the honest form of yes names what will not be delivered instead.
questions.mindset: Anyone may ask for anything, and one person still decides what the team does next.

questions.stem: A national driving-test booking service has been released fortnightly for ten months. The service desk has now refused to take first-line support, because none of the twenty released features has an operations runbook. Your team's definition of done covers code review, automated tests and deployment, and has never mentioned runbooks. The product owner wants the next three features before the summer peak. The head of operations wants the backlog stopped. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Add runbooks to the definition of done for future work and carry on with the next three features.
options.rationale: It fixes the leak and ignores the water on the floor. Twenty features remain unsupportable, and the operations refusal is about those, not about the ones not yet built.

options.text: Raise the missing documentation with the customer as a change request, since it was never in the agreed criteria.
options.rationale: Asking someone to fund work that a complete definition of done would always have included charges them for a gap in your own standard. It also frames operability as optional extra scope.

options.text: Add runbooks to the definition of done, size the missing documentation for released features as real backlog items, and have the product owner order them alongside new work with operations present.
options.rationale: It makes an invisible debt visible as work with a cost, and puts the sequencing decision in front of both people who have a claim on it. Neither party gets to settle it by refusing.

options.text: Have the team write all twenty runbooks before the next release, since the service cannot be supported without them.
options.rationale: It repays the whole debt in one lump on the team's own authority, ahead of a summer peak, without anyone weighing that against the features. Urgency does not make it the team's decision to take.

questions.explanation: A definition of done encodes what the organisation means by releasable, and anything missing from it accumulates silently across every increment until someone downstream refuses to accept the result. Repairing it has two parts that are easy to confuse: changing the standard, which is cheap, and discharging the debt already created, which is real work and must be ordered against everything else by the person who owns the ordering.
questions.mindset: When the standard was wrong, fix the standard and then treat what it missed as work somebody has to prioritise.

questions.stem: An animal shelter network's rehoming product has an epic titled "Improve the adopter experience" that has been open for fourteen months and now holds sixty-one items. New requests are added to it whenever nobody is sure where else they belong. Items range from a photo-cropping tool to a change in how home checks are recorded. Nothing in it has been delivered for two quarters. The product owner asks you how to tidy it up. What should the project manager suggest?

options.text: Split it into several smaller epics grouped by theme, so each becomes manageable.
options.rationale: Reorganising the container leaves the underlying question untouched: nobody has said what any of these items is for. Five tidy containers of unwanted work are no better than one untidy one.

options.text: Establish what outcome the epic was created to achieve, keep the items that serve it, and re-home or drop the rest.
options.rationale: It applies the only test that can shrink a backlog honestly, and it gives the survivors a shared reason to be ordered against other work. Items that fail the test were never going to be built anyway.

options.text: Delete the epic and leave the sixty-one items loose in the backlog.
options.rationale: This discards the only record of why the items were gathered while keeping all of the items. The backlog gets longer and less explicable at the same time.

options.text: Prioritise the epic as a single block so that it competes with other work as one unit.
options.rationale: A sixty-one item block cannot meaningfully be ordered against anything, because its value and cost are both unknowable. It will lose every comparison and stay open indefinitely.

questions.explanation: A container with a broad name and no stated outcome will attract anything nobody can place, and the drift is invisible because each individual addition seems reasonable. What restores it is not tidying but a decision about purpose, since purpose is the only thing that can justify removing an item somebody once asked for. A grouping that cannot say what it will change is a filing convenience rather than a piece of scope.
questions.mindset: Ask what a grouping of work is meant to change, and be willing to drop whatever does not serve it.

questions.stem: A cheese maker's trade ordering portal is built in two-week iterations. The team committed to six items totalling twenty-eight points at planning on Monday. On Wednesday the product owner asks to take out a five-point item that is no longer needed this month and bring in an eight-point item a large customer is waiting for. The team agrees the swap is feasible. Work out what the iteration now holds.

blanks.label: Points committed in the iteration after the swap
blanks.rationale: Twenty-eight less the five-point item removed, plus the eight-point item added, gives thirty-one. The arithmetic is trivial and is exactly what nobody does before agreeing to a swap.

blanks.label: Change in committed points, as a positive or negative number
blanks.rationale: The iteration has grown by three points, so this is not a like-for-like exchange. Calling a swap even when it is not is how iterations quietly become over-committed.

blanks.label: Where the removed item goes so it is not lost
blanks.rationale: Work pulled out of an iteration returns to the backlog to be ordered against everything else, rather than being deleted or held privately by the team.

questions.explanation: Changing the contents of an iteration is legitimate and routine, and it stays honest only if the arithmetic is done out loud: what came out, what went in, and whether the total moved. A swap described in words sounds symmetrical even when it adds capacity the team does not have, and the removed item needs a destination or it disappears from a decision nobody ever revisits.
questions.mindset: Do the arithmetic on a swap before agreeing to it, because two items exchanged are rarely equal.

questions.stem: Two decisions have landed on the same afternoon in the team building a village hall booking product, and in both cases people are looking at you rather than at the person whose decision it is. Neither decision is difficult once its owner is identified. Complete each sentence with the response that fits. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: Two department heads each insist their request must be in the next release and the team can build only one of them. The decision on which is built belongs to
The team believes an item cannot be called finished because it does not meet the standard the team holds all its work to, though it works. Whether the item is called done belongs to

options.text: the product owner, who orders the backlog on behalf of everyone asking
options.rationale: Competing requests are a value question, and a single accountable orderer is what stops the answer being decided by whoever escalates hardest. Both department heads get the same route.

options.text: the team, whose own standard is the one being applied
options.rationale: The definition of done is the team's professional standard, and a team that can be overruled on it stops maintaining one. Whether to release despite the shortfall is a separate question with a different owner.

options.text: the project manager, who is accountable for the release date
options.rationale: Not used. Accountability for a date is not authority over value or over craft standards, and a manager who takes either decision removes the ownership that makes both roles function.

questions.explanation: Scope questions in iterative delivery divide by who owns the consequence: what gets built next belongs to whoever is accountable for value, and what counts as finished belongs to the people who have to live with the work. Collapsing both into whoever is under the most schedule pressure produces fast decisions and hollow roles, and the standard is the first thing to go.
questions.mindset: Match each decision to whoever carries its consequence, not to whoever is most senior in the room.

questions.stem: Three items in a seed retailer's backlog have each been carried over once already because they are too large to finish inside an iteration, and each one resists splitting for a different underlying reason. The team wants a general rule; there is no general rule. Match each item to the way of splitting it that fits. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: Ordering works the same way for trade customers and for the public, except that trade customers get credit terms, bulk pricing and a purchase order field.
The stock availability display has to draw from the nursery system, the warehouse system and a third-party bulb supplier's feed, each with different data.
The checkout confirmation is small in behaviour but must work in English, Welsh, Polish, Romanian and Lithuanian before the team considers it finished.

options.text: Split by business rule variation, taking the simplest customer type end to end first
options.rationale: The journey is one journey with variations bolted on, so the simple case is a complete, usable slice and each variation is a separable increment that can be judged on its own value.

options.text: Split by data source, delivering one source working end to end before adding the others
options.rationale: Each source carries its own integration risk and its own surprises, and a display fed by one real source proves the whole path works. Doing all three at once means learning nothing until the end.

options.text: Split by acceptance criterion, taking one language to done and treating the remaining languages as separate items
options.rationale: The size lives entirely in a repeated criterion rather than in the behaviour, so the criteria are the natural seam. It also lets the team learn what translation actually costs before committing to five.

options.text: Split by technical layer, delivering the database work, then the service, then the interface
options.rationale: Not used. Layered slices cannot be demonstrated or accepted on their own, so feedback arrives only when the last one lands and every earlier slice is a promise rather than a result.

questions.explanation: An oversized item is usually large for a locatable reason: variations on one path, several sources behind one view, or a criterion repeated many times. Naming the reason points at the seam, and the test of any split is whether each piece could be shown to someone and judged. Splits chosen for the team's convenience rather than the item's structure produce pieces that only make sense together.
questions.mindset: Find why an item is big before deciding where to cut it, and check every piece could stand on its own.

questions.stem: A wind turbine maintenance firm's inspection app team pulled in a spike titled "investigate offline data capture" at the start of the last iteration. It has consumed most of two people's time for a fortnight. The engineers are enthusiastic and have prototyped three approaches, and they would like another iteration to compare them properly. No decision has been made and no product backlog item depends on the outcome yet. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Let the spike continue for another iteration, since the comparison is nearly complete and the work is genuinely useful.
options.rationale: Research without a decision date expands to fill whatever capacity it is given, and "nearly complete" is the normal state of an unbounded investigation. The cost is paid in features nobody discussed giving up.

options.text: Close the spike now with what is known, and require any future spike to name its question, its time box and the decision it will inform.
options.rationale: A spike exists to buy information for a pending decision, so stating the decision first is what makes the time box meaningful and what tells you when enough has been learned.

options.text: Convert the spike into an estimated story so it can be tracked like other work.
options.rationale: Estimating an unknown by treating it as known work is the error a spike exists to avoid, and it produces a number that will be wrong in an unpredictable direction.

options.text: Ask the engineers to write up their three approaches in a report for the team to review.
options.rationale: It rewards the investigation with more investigation and produces a document instead of a choice. The output of a spike should be a decision, not a paper.

questions.explanation: Investigative work is scope like any other and needs the same boundaries, but it is unusually easy to justify because it always feels informative. The discipline is to attach it to a decision that is waiting and to a fixed amount of time, so that the question of whether enough is known has an answer someone can give. Without that, a spike quietly becomes a research programme funded from delivery capacity.
questions.mindset: Buy information for a decision that is waiting, and fix in advance how much you will spend on it.

questions.stem: Two teams build a mail-order seed catalogue product from one shared backlog, pulling the next item they can take. This iteration both teams have separately built substitution handling for out-of-stock lines, in different ways, and neither noticed until the review. Roughly nine days of effort has been duplicated and one implementation must now be discarded. Both teams are annoyed and each thinks the other should have checked. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Split the backlog in two, giving each team its own list to work from.
options.rationale: Splitting one product's ordering into two lists creates two priorities and guarantees the teams optimise separately. It solves the collision by giving up the single view of value.

options.text: Keep one ordered backlog, make the team taking each item visible when it is pulled, and decide with both teams which implementation is kept.
options.rationale: The collision came from invisible pull rather than from shared ordering, so the fix belongs at the point of pulling. Settling the discarded implementation jointly stops the loss becoming a grievance.

options.text: Introduce a joint daily meeting between the two teams to coordinate what they are working on.
options.rationale: It answers an information problem with a recurring meeting, spending both teams' time every day to prevent something that a visible board would prevent for free.

options.text: Give one team the top half of the backlog and the other the bottom half.
options.rationale: An arbitrary partition means one team is systematically working on less valuable items, and it breaks whenever priority changes, which is constantly.

questions.explanation: Shared ordering is what keeps two teams pulling the most valuable work; shared visibility of who has taken what is what stops them colliding. The two are often confused, and the instinctive remedy of splitting the backlog sacrifices the first to fix the second. Where work is duplicated, look for what was invisible at the moment of pulling rather than for a rule about who owns which items.
questions.mindset: Keep one order of value and make it obvious who has picked up what.

questions.stem: A university library's catalogue team has been quietly folding restructuring work into feature items for several months, on the reasoning that the product owner would never prioritise it. Estimates have crept upwards and a straightforward feature now takes twice as long as a year ago. In a retrospective a developer says out loud that half of some items is invisible work. The product owner is in the room and looks surprised. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Make the restructuring work visible as items in the backlog, so its cost can be seen and ordered.
options.rationale: Work hidden inside estimates cannot be discussed, defended or traded off, and visibility is the precondition for every other decision about it. It also restores meaning to the feature estimates.

options.text: Agree with the product owner how much of each iteration's capacity goes to this work, rather than deciding it privately item by item.
options.rationale: It converts a series of concealed decisions into one negotiated policy that both sides can hold each other to, and gives the team a legitimate route instead of a covert one.

options.text: Stop the restructuring work and put the whole capacity into features until delivery speed recovers.
options.rationale: It mistakes the work for waste when the rising estimates are the evidence that it is needed. Speed recovers briefly and then falls further, and the team learns that honesty was punished.

options.text: Build a fixed padding factor into all future estimates to cover the work.
options.rationale: Padding keeps the work invisible while making every estimate less accurate, and it leaves the same conversation to be had again in a year with worse numbers.

options.text: Record it in a separate technical debt register that the team reviews each month.
options.rationale: A register only the team reads is not visibility; it is a private list. The work still competes with nothing and is still funded out of concealed estimate inflation.

questions.explanation: Internal work is real scope with a real cost, and the temptation to conceal it is strongest exactly where a product owner has shown no appetite for it. Concealment buys short-term peace and destroys the estimates everyone plans with, so the remedy is visibility first and then an explicit agreement about how much capacity it gets. A negotiated share can be argued about; a hidden one can only be discovered.
questions.mindset: Put the work you would rather not explain into the open, because hidden effort corrupts every number built on it.

questions.stem: The product owner for a lifeboat charity's volunteer scheduling product is on a three-week overseas assessment with no reliable contact. Before leaving she ordered the backlog but left several items with acceptance criteria that read as one-line intentions. Two days in, the team has begun writing its own criteria for the top item and plans to have the product owner confirm them on her return. The next iteration starts on Monday. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Let the team write the criteria and continue, confirming everything when the product owner is back.
options.rationale: It has the team deciding what the charity wants and then seeking ratification for three weeks of built work, which is the least reversible order to do it in.

options.text: Pause work on items with ambiguous criteria until the product owner returns.
options.rationale: Idling a team for three weeks treats an absence as unresolvable when a delegate or the ordered items with clear criteria could keep work moving.

options.text: Agree a named delegate with authority to clarify and accept, in writing; where none exists, work the items whose criteria are unambiguous and hold the rest.
options.rationale: It restores a decision-maker rather than a proxy, and the fallback sequences around the ambiguity instead of guessing through it. Naming the authority in writing is what makes later acceptance stand up.

options.text: Escalate the absence to the sponsor as a blocker to delivery.
options.rationale: Escalating before trying the obvious remedy spends attention on an announcement, and a planned absence with no delegate is a gap the project manager can close directly.

questions.explanation: A product owner's absence is a foreseeable event and the thing that must not lapse is the authority to say what is wanted and to accept what is built. Delegation with a name and a written mandate keeps that authority intact; a team quietly supplying it does not, however good its judgement, because the person who will live with the product has not agreed. Where no delegate exists, sequencing around the ambiguity is safer than resolving it by assumption.
questions.mindset: Cover an absence by naming who holds the authority, not by quietly acting in their place.

questions.stem: A ski lift operator's lift-pass team adopted a definition of ready after several iterations began with poorly understood items. It now runs to eleven conditions, including signed-off wireframes and a completed data mapping. Items wait an average of six weeks in a refinement queue before a team may start them, two analysts work full time preparing them, and half the prepared detail is out of date by the time work begins. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Abandon the definition of ready, since it has become a bottleneck.
options.rationale: It over-corrects back to the original problem of items nobody understood. The conditions were introduced for a reason and the reason has not gone away.

options.text: Keep it as a guide, cut it to what the team genuinely needs to begin, and refine items just before they are picked up rather than weeks ahead.
options.rationale: It preserves the purpose while removing the queue, and refining close to the work stops detail decaying before use. Treating the list as a guide rather than a gate is what allows judgement on the marginal item.

options.text: Add a third analyst so that items are prepared faster and the queue shortens.
options.rationale: Adding capacity to a queue nobody wants produces more prepared items that go stale. It also deepens the split between people who think and people who build.

options.text: Refine further ahead so that a larger buffer of ready items is always available.
options.rationale: A bigger buffer is more inventory of decisions taken early, and decisions taken early against a changing product are the ones most likely to be wrong when used.

questions.explanation: Entry criteria for work exist to prevent a specific failure, and they turn harmful when they become a gate ahead of a queue: the detail they produce ages, and the preparation becomes a separate stage with its own staff. Detail is perishable, so the value of refining something is highest shortly before it is built. The useful question about any readiness rule is what would actually go wrong if the team started without it.
questions.mindset: Prepare work close to when it will be done, because detail decided too early goes stale before it is used.

questions.stem: A national park authority's visitor infrastructure programme has a baselined scope statement for its construction workstreams and a product backlog for the two software teams. At the programme board, a member asks for a single answer to what the programme will deliver. Comparing the two records, you find the backlog contains items nobody has assessed against the baseline, and the baseline contains items the teams stopped building months ago. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Reconcile the two records item by item, separating approved changes that were never written back from additions that were never approved.
options.rationale: The two categories have different remedies: one is an administrative repair, the other is unapproved scope that needs a decision. Merging them into a single tidy-up would let real additions pass unexamined.

options.text: Agree one governing record for each workstream and a written rule for how a change in the backlog reaches the baseline.
options.rationale: Divergence recurs unless there is a route between the records, and naming the governing one per workstream stops both being partly authoritative. The rule is what keeps the reconciliation from being needed again next year.

options.text: Present the baselined scope statement to the board, since it is the approved record of what was agreed.
options.rationale: Presenting a document you know to be inaccurate protects a process at the board's expense. It also means the board approves progress against work that stopped months ago.

options.text: Present the backlog, since it reflects what the teams are actually doing.
options.rationale: Current is not the same as agreed. Showing the board the backlog treats work nobody approved as though it had authority simply because it is being built.

options.text: Ask the board to approve the current backlog as the new scope baseline.
options.rationale: It launders every unapproved addition through one approval that nobody can inspect item by item, and it rewards divergence with retrospective authority.

questions.explanation: Hybrid programmes routinely keep two records of scope, and they drift apart quietly because each is maintained by people who trust their own. The obligation is not to force one shape onto both workstreams but to keep a live route between them, so that a change in either can be traced to a decision. When a reconciliation is needed, distinguishing bookkeeping from unapproved scope is the whole value of the exercise.
questions.mindset: Two records of scope are workable only if there is a route between them that someone maintains.

questions.stem: Your contract with a dental group commits you to migrate all patient records into a new practice system. Discovery finds that around a third of the records predate the group's 2009 merger, hold no verified date of birth, and cannot be matched to a current patient. Migrating them would carry unverified clinical data into a live system. The clinical director wants everything moved; your delivery lead says a third of the records are not usable at any price. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Redefine the migration scope by the records' fitness and intended use, and have the client decide which classes are migrated, archived or retired.
options.rationale: It replaces a volume commitment with a decision the client is competent to take, class by class, on clinical and legal grounds. All records is not a specification once a third of them cannot support the use they were bought for.

options.text: Treat the changed understanding as a change to the agreed scope, with the discovery evidence, and price and plan it explicitly.
options.rationale: The contract was written on an assumption about the data that discovery has disproved, and both parties need that on the record before anyone spends more. Evidence is what turns a claim about the data into a shared basis for deciding.

options.text: Migrate everything as the contract requires and flag the unverified records inside the new system.
options.rationale: It satisfies the words of the contract while delivering a clinical system holding unverifiable patient data, which is the outcome the contract existed to buy the opposite of. Compliance is not the same as delivery.

options.text: Cleanse the unmatched third at your own cost to avoid a contractual argument.
options.rationale: Absorbing a material change to avoid a difficult conversation sets the precedent for everything discovery turns up next, and the cleansing needs clinical decisions your team has no standing to make anyway.

options.text: Exclude the unmatched records and record the exclusion in the project's assumptions log.
options.rationale: Unilateral removal of a contractual commitment, recorded somewhere the client does not read, is the version of this that ends in a dispute at acceptance.

questions.explanation: A scope commitment expressed as a volume assumes something about the material that may turn out to be false, and discovery that disproves it changes what was actually agreed, whatever the wording says. Delivering the letter of such a commitment can defeat its purpose entirely. The route through is to re-express the scope in terms of use and fitness, put the evidence in front of the party who owns the consequences, and let the change be decided rather than absorbed or imposed.
questions.mindset: When the material turns out to be different, reopen the commitment rather than delivering its words.

questions.stem: A coach operator has contracted your organisation on an outcome basis: reduce missed departures caused by driver scheduling to under one per cent within a year, with payment tied to the result. Your delivery team keeps asking which features are in scope, and your account manager has started drafting a feature list to give them certainty. The client has deliberately not specified a solution and expects you to find one. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Complete the feature list, agree it with the client and baseline it so everyone knows what is being built.
options.rationale: It converts an outcome contract back into a feature contract and gives away the freedom that was bought and paid for. Once a list is agreed, delivering it becomes the measure of success even if departures are still missed.

options.text: Hold the outcome as the scope, maintain a live list of the work currently believed necessary to reach it, and re-decide that list as evidence arrives.
options.rationale: It gives the team something concrete to work from without freezing a guess made before anything was learned. Explicitly labelling the list as current belief is what keeps it revisable when the data says otherwise.

options.text: Let each team decide feature by feature what to build, since only the outcome is contracted.
options.rationale: Without a shared statement of what is currently believed necessary, nobody can plan, cost or coordinate, and the outcome becomes an aspiration attached to uncoordinated work.

options.text: Ask the client to specify the features they expect, so that the delivery team has certainty.
options.rationale: It asks the client to supply the solution they deliberately withheld, and any answer they give becomes a constraint that also transfers the risk of the wrong solution back to them.

questions.explanation: Where the commitment is to a result rather than a list, scope is still needed for planning but has a different status: it is the current best theory of how the result will be achieved, not a promise about what will exist. Recording it that way lets a team work concretely while remaining able to abandon work that the evidence stops supporting. Baselining a theory as though it were a commitment forfeits the flexibility that outcome-based contracting exists to create.
questions.mindset: When the deal is about a result, treat the feature list as your current theory rather than your promise.
