questions.stem: A bakery chain is piloting a stock ordering tool in three of its ninety shops to find out whether shop managers will use it instead of phoning orders in. Six weeks in, the regional manager and two shop managers have asked for a supplier invoice reconciliation feature, a loyalty tie-in and multi-site reporting, all described as necessary before rollout. The pilot has four weeks left and a decision meeting booked. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Add the requested features, since they will be needed for rollout and building them now saves time later.
options.rationale: It converts a pilot into an early rollout build and spends the remaining weeks on features that only matter if the answer turns out to be yes. The question the pilot exists to answer goes unanswered.

options.text: Hold the pilot to the question it exists to answer, and keep the rollout requests in a separate list for the decision that follows.
options.rationale: It protects the four weeks that will actually inform the decision while losing none of the requests. The separate list also becomes useful evidence about what rollout would cost if the pilot succeeds.

options.text: Refuse all changes to the pilot so that its results are not contaminated.
options.rationale: A pilot that cannot respond to what it learns about its own question is not a pilot. Changes that help managers use the tool are exactly what should be allowed.

options.text: Extend the pilot to more shops so that the additional features can be tested properly.
options.rationale: Widening the trial answers a different and larger question, delays the decision it was scoped to support, and increases the cost of a no.

questions.explanation: A pilot is scoped by the question it must answer, not by what the eventual product will need, and requests to make it rollout-ready are the most common way that scope is lost. Keeping the boundary means separating changes that serve the question from changes that presume the answer. The requests themselves are valuable and should be captured, because they describe the scope of a decision that has not yet been taken.
questions.mindset: Scope a trial to the question it must answer, and hold everything that assumes the answer.

questions.stem: A water utility's meter reading replacement is three months from cutover. The scope statement describes the new system in detail and says nothing about retiring the old one: its two remaining interfaces, its seven years of readings held under a retention obligation, and the four staff whose roles exist to operate it. Nobody has costed or scheduled any of that. Your sponsor's view is that decommissioning is business as usual. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Add the decommissioning work to your own scope so that the gap is covered before cutover.
options.rationale: Taking on unfunded work to be helpful hides the fact that nobody decided who owns it, and it commits your team to retention obligations and staffing questions it has no authority over.

options.text: Name the retirement as work needing an owner, a funding source and a decision date, and get the boundary recorded in a baselined document even if the owner is not you.
options.rationale: It forces a decision while there is still time to act, and recording the boundary protects both sides afterwards. Being clear that something is out of your scope is only safe once somebody else's scope contains it.

options.text: Raise decommissioning as a risk to cutover in the next report.
options.rationale: It is a certainty rather than a risk: the old system exists and will still exist at cutover. Filing a known gap as a risk defers it by a reporting cycle and dilutes the register.

options.text: Accept the sponsor's view and assume operations will absorb the retirement as routine work.
options.rationale: This is the assumption that created the gap, restated with more confidence. Operations has not been asked, resourced or given the retention obligation, and none of that changes by agreeing with the sponsor.

questions.explanation: Replacing something is two pieces of work, and the second one is chronically left out because it produces nothing anyone wants to look at. Whether it belongs inside the project is a legitimate question; whether someone owns it is not optional. The useful discipline at a boundary is to insist that work sits inside somebody's baseline before agreeing it sits outside yours, because unowned work at cutover becomes the project's problem regardless of the document.
questions.mindset: Work is only out of your scope once it is demonstrably inside somebody else's.

questions.stem: A farm shop network's new click-and-collect platform has a first release containing every feature in the approved scope, delivered over nine months. The commercial director has begun describing this release to the board and to suppliers as the minimum viable product, with a bigger release to follow. Two board members have started asking why a minimum product is taking nine months, and one has suggested cutting it back. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Leave the label alone, since what matters is the content of the release rather than what people call it.
options.rationale: A label sets expectations about size, cost and how much can be cut, and this one invites a board to trim a release nobody has assessed. Words that mislead a decision-maker are not harmless.

options.text: Get agreement on what the first release must achieve and what is genuinely deferrable, then let the sponsor call it whatever they prefer.
options.rationale: It moves the argument from vocabulary to substance and produces something the board can act on. Once the deferrable content is named, the label stops carrying the decision.

options.text: Correct the terminology publicly so that the board understands the release is not a minimum viable product.
options.rationale: Winning a definitional argument in front of a board embarrasses the sponsor and still leaves the underlying question of what the release must contain unanswered.

options.text: Cut the release back so that it genuinely is a minimum viable product.
options.rationale: Reshaping approved scope to fit a word chosen carelessly lets vocabulary drive a delivery decision that should be driven by what the business needs first.

questions.explanation: Borrowed labels arrive carrying expectations their user did not intend to import, and the damage shows up as decisions taken on the strength of the word rather than the content. Arguing about the term is rarely productive; establishing what the release must achieve and what could wait converts the disagreement into a decision someone can take. Let the sponsor keep their language once the substance underneath it is agreed.
questions.mindset: Argue about what the release must achieve, not about what it should be called.

questions.stem: A commercial laundry's route planning programme baselined 148 requirements at the end of definition. Since then the change authority has approved additions of 12 requirements and the removal of 5. Two further requirements have been requested by the depot managers and assessed but not yet approved. Your PMO asks you to confirm the current position before the quarterly review. Work out what the numbers are.

blanks.label: Requirements in the current baseline
blanks.rationale: 148 plus 12 approved additions less 5 approved removals is 155. Only approved changes move a baseline, which is why the requested pair does not appear in this figure.

blanks.label: Requirements requested but not in any baseline
blanks.rationale: The two assessed but unapproved requests are visible work in progress and nothing more. Counting them in the baseline is how projects come to believe they owe things nobody agreed to.

blanks.label: The artifact that must be updated for each approved change so the requirement can still be traced to the work that delivers it
blanks.rationale: A change to the baseline that is not carried into the traceability record leaves a requirement with no link to a deliverable or a test, which is exactly the state in which requirements are silently dropped.

questions.explanation: A requirements baseline is a count of what has been agreed at a point in time, and it moves only through approved change; anything else in circulation is a request. Keeping the distinction visible stops a project quietly acquiring obligations from assessments and conversations. The corresponding discipline is to carry every approved change through into the record that links requirements to the work and the tests, because a requirement that loses its link is one nobody notices missing.
questions.mindset: Count only what has been approved, and carry every approved change through to the record that tracks it.

questions.stem: The diagram is the story map for a campsite group's booking product. The backbone across the top is the customer's journey, and beneath each step sit the items that support it. Four candidate first releases have been drawn. The programme needs a release that lets a real customer book and arrive at a pitch unaided, as early as possible. Select the candidate release that meets that condition.

graphic.title: Story map with journey backbone and four candidate release slices
graphic.caption: Select a candidate release. Use Tab or the arrow keys to move between them, then Enter or Space.

regions.label: Release A — search, choose pitch, pay, amend and check-in: every item under all five steps
regions.rationale: It certainly works, and it is everything, so it answers the question of what a complete product looks like rather than what an early usable release looks like. Choosing it abandons the word early in the condition.

regions.label: Release B — the top item under each of the five journey steps
regions.rationale: A thin slice across every step of the backbone is the smallest set that lets a customer get all the way from searching to arriving. Each step is covered at its simplest, which is what makes the journey complete rather than the features rich.

regions.label: Release C — every item under search and choose pitch, nothing under the later steps
regions.rationale: Depth in the first two steps builds an excellent way to browse pitches that nobody can book. Completing steps one at a time is the most common misreading of a map, because it looks like orderly progress.

regions.label: Release D — every item under pay and check-in, nothing under the earlier steps
regions.rationale: Starting at the technically difficult end delivers payment and arrival for a booking that cannot be made. It is attractive because it retires the hardest work first, which is a risk argument rather than a usable-release argument.

questions.explanation: A story map is read across before it is read down: the backbone is the journey somebody has to complete, and a release that omits any step of it cannot be used by anyone however much depth it has elsewhere. Slicing thinly across all steps produces something crude that works end to end, which can be put in front of real users; slicing deeply into a few steps produces something polished that cannot. Depth is added later, once the journey exists.
questions.mindset: Cut a release across the whole journey, not down into the parts that interest you most.

questions.stem: Three deliverables on a port authority's terminal programme are ready for acceptance in the same month, and your delivery director has suggested that you sign for all three yourself to save time before the quarter closes. Each one in fact needs a different authority to accept it. Match each deliverable to who should accept it. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: The latest increment of the haulier booking front end, demonstrated at the fortnightly review.
The migrated container movement balances that the finance team will report externally from next quarter.
The crane interlock interface, which forms part of the site safety case.

options.text: The product owner
options.rationale: Incremental product decisions belong to the person accountable for the product's value, and accepting at the review is what keeps the feedback loop short enough to be useful.

options.text: The finance controller named in the acceptance plan
options.rationale: The person who will be answerable for the reported figures is the one who must be satisfied they are right, since acceptance here transfers a reporting liability rather than a piece of software.

options.text: The independent safety assessor
options.rationale: Where a deliverable forms part of a safety case, acceptance has to come from someone independent of delivery, because the value of the assurance is precisely that it is not given by the people who built it.

options.text: The project manager, as the person accountable for delivery
options.rationale: Not used. Accountability for delivering work is not authority to accept it; a project manager who accepts their own team's output removes the independent check that acceptance exists to provide.

questions.explanation: Acceptance authority follows the consequence rather than the artifact: whoever will carry the liability, the risk or the value of a deliverable is the person whose agreement makes it accepted. That is why one programme can legitimately have several acceptance routes running at once, and why the fastest available signature is so often the wrong one. Naming the authority per deliverable in advance is what prevents the question being settled under deadline pressure.
questions.mindset: The right person to accept something is whoever has to live with it afterwards.

questions.stem: A charity operating sixty shops is replacing its donation and gift-aid recording system. The scope statement runs to eleven pages on the system and one line reading "business readiness" to cover redesigning the shop process, training three hundred volunteers and moving them off paper forms. The benefit case depends entirely on volunteers recording donations correctly at the counter. Go-live is in five months. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Proceed as scoped, since business readiness is properly the charity's own responsibility rather than the project's.
options.rationale: It may well belong to the charity, but leaving the half of the scope that carries the benefit undefined and unowned means nobody is planning it. Correct allocation is not the same as somebody doing it.

options.text: Break the business change into deliverables with owners and acceptance criteria, to the same standard as the system scope, whoever ends up delivering them.
options.rationale: Definition is what makes the work plannable and its absence visible, and it can be done regardless of who holds the budget. It also lets the charity see the size of what it has taken on.

options.text: Add volunteer training to the system supplier's contract so that it is covered by someone.
options.rationale: It buys training from a party who does not own the shop process and cannot decide how it should change. The gap is closed on paper by the least informed available party.

options.text: Defer the business readiness work until the system is stable in production.
options.rationale: Readiness cannot be retrofitted after go-live: three hundred volunteers will meet the system on day one, and their first experience of it sets the recording behaviour the benefits depend on.

questions.explanation: Where a benefit depends on people working differently, the change to how they work is scope, and it is chronically under-defined because it produces nothing a supplier invoices for. A one-line placeholder gives the appearance of coverage while making the work impossible to plan, estimate or accept. Defining it to the same standard as the technical scope is worth doing even when the deliverables belong to someone else, because that is what reveals whether anyone is actually doing them.
questions.mindset: Define the human half of the change as carefully as the technical half, because that is where the benefit lives.
